questions.q: What is the Windows service name for SQL Server Agent on a named instance?
options: SQLSERVERAGENT (same as a default instance)
MSSQL$<InstanceName>
sqlservr.exe
SQLAgent$<InstanceName>
questions.explain: A default instance's Agent service is SQLSERVERAGENT; a named instance's is SQLAgent$<InstanceName>, separate from the Engine service MSSQL$<InstanceName>.

questions.q: Where does SQL Server Agent store its job, schedule, and history configuration?
options: In a text config file next to sqlservr.exe
In the Windows Registry only
In tempdb, so it resets on every restart
In tables inside the msdb system database
questions.explain: Agent's configuration lives in msdb tables like sysjobs, sysjobsteps, sysschedules, sysoperators, sysalerts, and sysjobhistory — the SSMS GUI just reads/writes these.

questions.q: A nightly job didn't run, but the Database Engine is healthy and queries work fine. What does this lesson say about that scenario?
options: Agent runs as an independent service and can be stopped while the Engine keeps serving queries normally
It means msdb is corrupted
This is impossible — Agent and the Engine always start and stop together
It means the job's T-SQL step has a syntax error
questions.explain: Agent is architecturally separate from the Engine service; a healthy Engine doesn't guarantee Agent is even running, so an unrun job should prompt checking the Agent service first.

questions.q: Which msdb table holds the execution history for job runs?
options: msdb.dbo.sysjobs
msdb.dbo.sysalerts
msdb.dbo.sysjobhistory
msdb.dbo.sysoperators
questions.explain: sysjobhistory logs every job run; sysjobs just defines the job itself, not its run history.

questions.q: In Agent's object model, what is the relationship between an alert and a job?
options: An alert is just another name for a job step
Alerts can only be created after a job has run successfully once
They are related but independent — most jobs have no alert, and most alerts aren't tied to a job
Every job must have at least one alert defined
questions.explain: Alerts watch for a condition (error number or severity) and can notify an operator or run a job, but the two object types are independent — one doesn't require the other.
